frus-1969-76ve09p1-d21.summary: This is a long study prepared on July 6, 1973 by a State Department-led interagency group for the White House (under NSSM 185) on U.S. policy toward Libya. It reviews the Qadhafi regime, U.S. interests (oil, about 2,800 American citizens in Libya, Libya's strategic position) and options ranging from improving relations to confrontation. It notes that relations were at a low point after Libyan fighters fired on an American reconnaissance plane near Tripoli and an American oil company was nationalized.
tripoli_details: Libya declared a 'restricted area' within a 100-mile radius of Tripoli International Airport and claimed the right to control aircraft and ships entering it.
On 21 March 1973 Libyan fighter aircraft fired at an unarmed USAF C-130 reconnaissance plane flying inside that zone.

The study says diplomats and couriers accredited in Tripoli were denied entry because their passports lacked an Arabic translation, and American Embassy personnel could not leave since replacements could not be sent.
It expected that a Libyan-Egyptian union would reduce embassies in Tripoli to a lower status.
It records that Libyans demonstrated in June 1967 and February 1973 but otherwise showed little political activism.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d134.summary: On July 30, 1980 the State Department's Executive Secretary, Peter Tarnoff, sent Brzezinski a history of U.S.-Libyan relations from the 1969 revolution to 1980. It says relations stayed troubled, with brief hopes of improvement in 1975 and 1979, and explains the U.S. decisions to keep only a chargé d'affaires in Tripoli and to block sales of military aircraft such as C-130s.
tripoli_details: After Wheelus Air Force Base was forced to close in June 1970, the Embassy found it nearly impossible to get appointments with anyone but middle-level Foreign Ministry officials.
In early 1973 the U.S. decided to keep an official presence in Tripoli headed by a chargé d'affaires rather than an ambassador.
In April 1975 Libya said it had lifted the ceiling on U.S. Embassy personnel in Tripoli.
Under Secretary Newsom met Major Jallud in Tripoli in June 1979 for frank but promising talks.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d74.summary: This is National Intelligence Estimate 36.5-71 of April 30, 1971, assessing Libyan policy under the Revolutionary Command Council (RCC). Analysts judged the 28-year-old Colonel Qadhafi's regime was secure enough to last, that it had won popular credit by evicting Western bases and raising oil income, and that it was turning to Egypt, France and the Soviet bloc for military help.
tripoli_details: The estimate says the Tripolitanean Police and the Cyrenaican Defense Force were disbanded because they might have been focal points for discontent.
It reports that expelling the resident Italian community (15,000-20,000 people) in mid-1970 removed most skilled artisans and modern-sector farmers in Tripolitania.
It says a handful of Egyptians were at Ukbah Bin Nafi (formerly Wheelus) Air Base, used by the Libyan Air Force.
It says Cairo received about $160 million from Tripoli in the last year.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d53.summary: In Telegram 10936 of August 14, 1976, the U.S. Embassy in Cairo told Kissinger that Egypt's President Sadat had decided Qadhafi was a dangerous 'lunatic' who must be removed. The embassy described Egyptian troops massing on the Libyan border and weighed Egypt's options, from engineering a coup to a limited or full military attack.
tripoli_details: The embassy said assassination squads targeting Egyptian notables were first sent from Tripoli in summer 1975.
It reported that Egyptian forces in the western desert (over 10,000 troops) could, with reinforcements, mount an attack as far as Tripoli under favorable conditions.
One option it listed was a brigade-size airborne raid on Tripoli to destroy Qadhafi and his government.
It said Egypt was still sending a new ambassador to Tripoli despite Qadhafi's threat to sever relations on September 1.
It cited an August 8 bomb attack in central Cairo as the latest Libyan terrorist action.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d100.summary: This June 1, 1979 CIA intelligence memorandum, 'Libya's Changing Role as a Patron State,' judges that Qadhafi remained a major patron of terrorists but had changed tactics since late 1977 to improve his image in the West. It reports reduced help to Irish and European groups and some cooperation with Western governments.
tripoli_details: Libya invited the head of the State Department's Office for Combatting Terrorism to visit Tripoli, and the visit took place in January 1979.
The memo says an Italian claimed to have seen underwater training of Red Brigades members at a facility outside Tripoli.
It says 'Carlos' was housed at 'The Institute,' a terrorist training camp near Tripoli.
It counts 12 terrorist training camps in Libya in 1979, at least four used by Palestinian groups, compared with 20 in 1970.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d54.summary: This September 1, 1976 State Department intelligence report, 'Qadhafi: The Increased Threat,' argues that Qadhafi had moved beyond isolated terrorist acts and could now destabilize the Middle East and Africa, citing his $7 billion yearly oil revenue. It lists Libyan-backed plots against Sudan's Numayri, Egypt, Tunisia and others, and Libyan support for Uganda's Idi Amin.
tripoli_details: A senior Egyptian diplomat in Tripoli said Qadhafi was determined to topple Sudan's Numayri.
Libyan officials arrested two Egyptian security men on August 24 aboard a chartered Egypt Air flight from Cairo to Tripoli, which Egypt called 'an act of air piracy.'
The report says Tripoli sent radar equipment to Uganda and may have sent troops.
Libyan commando teams were caught in operations to kidnap or assassinate Libyan opponents abroad, including the nominal Foreign Minister in Rome.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d32.summary: This August 19, 1974 CIA intelligence memorandum examines the growing feud between Libya's Qadhafi and Egypt's Sadat. It says Sadat had recalled Egypt's ambassador and withdrawn Egypt's military mission from Libya, that Qadhafi was increasingly isolated, and that the Soviets were improving ties with Libya through a major arms deal.
tripoli_details: Sadat recalled Egypt's ambassador and withdrew the entire Egyptian military mission in Libya.
The memo says the Libyan people were happy to see the Egyptians go, though many educated Libyans understood Libya's dependence on Egyptian goodwill.
Jallud visited Moscow in May 1974 and Libya concluded a major arms deal with the Soviet Union.
Sadat offered to send an emissary to Tripoli for reconciliation talks.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d131.summary: This May 16, 1980 CIA intelligence memorandum judges that Libya might be entering a more dangerous phase of support for terrorism. It points to the November 1979 burning of the U.S. embassy in Tripoli, Qadhafi's feud with moderate Palestinians, and his willingness to target heads of state.
tripoli_details: The April 1980 summit of the Steadfastness and Confrontation Front was held in Tripoli.
The memo calls the sacking of the U.S. embassy in Tripoli in November 1979 a crude imitation of the seizure of the U.S. embassy in Tehran.
It also mentions the burning of the French embassy in Tripoli.
Libyans reportedly trained dissidents from Tanzania, Rwanda, Mozambique, South Africa and Namibia at a camp south of Tripoli.
Qadhafi hindered a Cuban effort to move Ugandan cadets to Havana via Tripoli.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d77.summary: This May 17, 1971 memorandum is a CIA status report on Libya covering the period from early 1971. It describes the effect of Nasser's death, Soviet tanks arriving in Tripoli, the successful oil-company settlements, and at least seven counter-coup attempts in the first sixteen months after the revolution.
tripoli_details: Soviet tanks and other military hardware arrived in Tripoli on 18 July 1970.
Negotiations with Western oil companies opened in Tripoli in late February 1971 and were completed on 2 April, giving a five-year agreement.
The report says at least seven counter-coup attempts occurred within Libya in the first sixteen months after the revolution, plus one launched from Chad.
CIA was monitoring two further counter-coup plans, one led by former Libyan military officers abroad.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d101.summary: This is the record of a June 17, 1979 meeting in Tripoli between Under Secretary of State David Newsom and Major Abd al-Salam Jallud, described as number two to Colonel Qadhafi. Newsom explained the U.S. interest in better relations, while Jallud said Libya would not change its position on the Palestinian issue to improve bilateral ties.
tripoli_details: The meeting took place in Tripoli on June 17, 1979 as part of the Newsom mission.
Jallud said the mission followed a Palestinian meeting held in Tripoli.
Marshall Tito had recently visited Tripoli and passed Qadhafi's comments about lack of contact with the U.S.
Madfai was the Libyan chargé d'affaires who responded quickly to the U.S. proposal.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d45.summary: These are minutes of a November 24, 1969 Washington Special Actions Group meeting on Libya, shortly after the coup. Officials discussed contingency plans, including a military-supported evacuation of Americans, and the coming talks on the future of Wheelus Air Base starting December 15.
tripoli_details: Newsom said the planned evacuation of U.S. citizens would have U.S. forces enter through Wheelus.
The Libyans would not permit resumption of training activities at Wheelus and wanted the U.S. to withdraw, so the best the U.S. could expect was about one more year there.
Unarmed aircraft were still operating in and out of Wheelus, but the U.S. Phantoms stationed there were embarrassing to the Libyan government.
Talks with the Libyans on Wheelus were to begin December 15.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d25.summary: On September 17, 1973 Assistant Secretary Newsom sent Kissinger a follow-on options paper on U.S. policy toward Libya (NSSM 185). It weighs continuing present policy, sending a special emissary, or harsher steps, and warns that tougher options could lead Libya to close the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli.
tripoli_details: One option was to keep a small mission going in Tripoli without accrediting a new ambassador.
The paper warned that some options could result in Libyan closure of the American Embassy in Tripoli and nationalization of remaining U.S. oil assets.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d44.summary: On November 20, 1969 NSC staff members Behr and Saunders sent Kissinger a summary and critique of a paper on possible pressures against Libya's new regime. It covers the Wheelus base question, the regime's insecurity, and U.S. oil investment valued at $5 billion, and weighs options such as delaying a reply on Wheelus or cutting oil purchases.
tripoli_details: The Libyans asked the U.S. to leave Wheelus before December 24, 1971; the U.S. planned to agree in principle to early withdrawal and propose detailed discussions.
The paper said a delay on Wheelus could lead the regime to open a street campaign endangering the U.S. community, base and Embassy.
It noted that the former King had moved to Egypt that month and the Crown Prince was in jail, and that other possible contenders were under surveillance in Benghazi.
It said 90 percent of Libya's 3 million barrels a day was produced by twenty-eight American companies.
A landing of forces at Wheelus was listed as an option to consider for evacuating Americans.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d50.summary: This December 30, 1969 National Intelligence Estimate, 'Short-Term Prospects for Libya,' assesses the new Revolutionary Command Council shortly after the September coup. Analysts judged the council wanted to remove the Western bases at Wheelus, Tobruk and El Adem, had no clear program beyond that, and had not sought close ties with the USSR.
tripoli_details: The estimate says the 6,000 US and British military personnel in the country at the time of the revolution were seen as a potential threat to Libya, whose armed forces numbered only about 8,000.
It judged the Libyans intended to use Wheelus as a military airfield and might hire civilian contractors or ask Egypt for technicians to run it.
It reported that a Soviet offer of military assistance made right after the revolution was rejected.
Soviet diplomats complained of difficulty reaching RCC members and of harassment by low-ranking Libyan military personnel.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d106.summary: In this October 4, 1979 cable, Secretary of State Vance reported his 45-minute talk in New York with Libyan Foreign Minister Turayki. Vance said the U.S. did not want to undermine the Libyan government but objected to Libyan support for terrorism, and he proposed exchanging high-level visits and cultural exchanges.
tripoli_details: Vance hoped a senior official such as Saunders or Newsom could visit Tripoli soon.
Turayki praised U.S. Chargé Eagleton for strengthening relations in Tripoli and suggested a committee based in Tripoli to review bilateral relations.

frus-1981-88v24-d66.summary: In this January 30, 1986 cable the U.S. Embassy in Algiers reported on a meeting between Algerian leaders and Qadhafi in a remote desert location, at which Qadhafi asked Algeria to pass a message to the United States. The embassy said Algeria saw the meeting as a success because it controlled the media and gained concessions on Tunisia and the Western Sahara.
tripoli_details: The embassy said the remote desert location let the Algerians prevent any pro-Qadhafi demonstrations.
It said Algeria obtained concessions from Qadhafi on Tunisia, support for Ben Bella and the Western Sahara.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d94.summary: In Telegram 1699 of October 30, 1972, the departing U.S. Ambassador to Libya, Joseph Palmer, reported a farewell meeting of an hour and a half with Qadhafi at his office in the Aliziya barracks. Qadhafi complained the U.S. had not delivered on contracts and armed Israel, while Prime Minister Jallud said the Palestine cause was a matter of life and death.
tripoli_details: The meeting took place on the evening of October 28, 1972 in Qadhafi's office at the Aliziya barracks.
Present were Prime Minister Jallud, Foreign Minister Kikhya, Chief of Staff Abu Bayr Yunis and RCC member Hamza.
Qadhafi said the evacuation of Wheelus had been resolved more easily than expected.
The day before, Qadhafi spoke at an intellectuals' seminar in Tripoli about steering clear of major powers.

frus-1981-88v24-d10.summary: In this August 10, 1981 cable, the U.S. Embassy in Algiers reported that Algeria's Foreign Ministry asked for U.S. views on rising tension between Libya and Egypt/Sudan. Algeria planned to send a high-level delegation to Tripoli to urge moderation on Qadhafi and feared a superpower confrontation.
tripoli_details: The Algerians planned to send a very high-level delegation to Tripoli in a week or ten days to press Libya to be more conciliatory.
The embassy judged Algeria feared a U.S. move against Qadhafi directly or through Egypt and Sudan.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d22.summary: These are minutes of an August 14, 1973 Senior Review Group meeting on U.S. policy toward Libya, chaired by Kissinger. Participants debated whether to send an emissary, punish Libya or buy it off, and discussed a cable from the U.S. mission in Tripoli arguing against approving new military equipment for Libya.
tripoli_details: Kissinger referred to Tripoli telegram 1044 of August 13, in which the chargé argued against approving new military equipment for Libya without getting something besides money.
Sisco suggested loosening relations with Libya and coordinating with oil companies to apply leverage on Qadhafi.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d104.summary: On August 7, 1979 CIA's National Foreign Assessment Center director Bowie sent Brzezinski a note assessing nationalized American oil assets in Libya and compensation. The CIA expected disputes between Tripoli and the companies over valuation and judged Libya could replace U.S. technical services with European firms.
tripoli_details: The note says Libya could probably get good terms by giving non-U.S. firms access to crude denied to the nationalized U.S. companies.
It expected valuation disputes between Tripoli and the companies.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d44.summary: On July 7, 1975 NSC staffer Robert Oakley sent Scowcroft a memo, 'The Libyan Threat,' drawing on a CIA study of the Soviet-Libyan arms relationship. It reported a major expansion of Soviet arms deals including jets, bombers, submarines and tanks, and Soviet port-call rights.
tripoli_details: Kosygin recently visited Tripoli.
Tripoli apparently agreed to allow Soviet ships occasional port calls for bunkering and replenishment under tight Libyan controls.
The Libyans may be dangling greater concessions such as base rights to get Soviet help in building naval facilities at Tobruk.

frus-1981-88v24-d159.summary: This April 20, 1986 cable from the U.S. Embassy in Algiers reports Algerian reaction to the U.S. strikes on Libya. An Algerian official said Algeria had sent a party official to Tripoli to warn Qadhafi about terrorism just before the strikes and that Qadhafi had denied involvement.
tripoli_details: Party Permanent Secretary Messaadia was sent to Tripoli to warn Qadhafi on terrorism just before the U.S. strikes, according to Belkheir.
Belkheir said news of the strikes had mobilized Algerian public opinion on Qadhafi's side and that he banned TV coverage of foreign demonstrations.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d63.summary: This July 31, 1970 CIA intelligence memorandum reviews where Libya got its weapons after the 1969 revolution. It says Britain had been the main supplier, that U.S. military aid ran from 1957 to 1970, and that the Soviet Union suddenly delivered tanks and artillery on 18 July 1970.
tripoli_details: Wheelus Air Base was handed over to the Libyans on 11 June 1970, after which the U.S. military aid group was reduced to a five-man liaison section attached to the U.S. Embassy.
The Soviet Union made an overt delivery of tanks and artillery on 18 July 1970.
A special envoy from the Soviet Defense Ministry visited Tripoli as early as 19 September 1969.
The memo says U.S. military aid to Libya from 1957 to 1970 totaled about $33 million, and Libya's fleet included nine F-5s and three C-130s among 30 aircraft.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d71.summary: In Telegram 373 of February 24, 1971, the U.S. Ambassador in Tripoli reported a 1 hour 45 minute meeting with Qadhafi at the Aziziyah barracks. Qadhafi said the only real issue between the two countries was the Arab-Israeli dispute, but he still wanted the F-5 aircraft the U.S. had not delivered.
tripoli_details: The meeting was held February 23, 1971 at the Aziziyah barracks, with Foreign Minister Kikhya and Marthinsen the only others present.
Qadhafi arrived in casual sport attire and was relaxed and cordial.
Qadhafi said young officers had been optimistic when the U.S. Air Force evacuated Wheelus that good relations would follow.
The telegram was repeated to the consulate in Benghazi.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d90.summary: On July 28, 1972 Deputy Secretary of State Irwin sent Secretary Rogers an action memorandum on Libya. Irwin said he favored delivering the F-5 aircraft the U.S. had contracted to sell, without demanding anything specific on the oil company dispute, to remove an irritant and open the way to less hostile talks.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d94.summary: In this September 21, 1978 cable the State Department told the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli to be cautious about reports of Qadhafi's interest in better relations. It said the U.S. would keep refusing senior-level talks, but would consult Congress on selling two Boeing 727s with guarantees they be used only commercially.
tripoli_details: The Department said it was pleased the embassy was setting up a channel to Qadhafi.
It warned the Libyans that ad hominem attacks on President Carter or injury to U.S. persons or property would be resented by Congress.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d125.summary: On February 1, 1980 Secretary of State Vance sent President Carter a memo on the future of the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli. He recommended keeping the mission at its minimum size of eight or fewer, offering only minimal consular services until after the exchange of Egyptian and Israeli ambassadors, because of the risk of another attack like the one on December 2.
tripoli_details: The U.S. chargé returned to Tripoli December 31, 1979 expecting to be received by Qadhafi, but there had been no response to Carter's January 17 message.
The memo says the weight of intelligence evidence suggested Qadhafi himself authorized the December 2 attack on the Embassy to prove his government was as 'revolutionary' as the Iranians.
Vance recommended the mission stay at eight people or fewer and reexamine its status in mid-March.
An Afro-Arab meeting planned in Tripoli that month was postponed because Libya insisted on excluding Egypt.
Vance proposed delivering the President's message to the Foreign Minister if Qadhafi would not receive Chargé Eagleton.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d96.summary: On December 13, 1972 the State Department's Deputy Assistant Secretary Ross wrote about the Libyan Ambassador's alleged involvement in terrorism after an FBI report. Attached is an Embassy Tripoli airgram saying the Tripoli newspaper al-Fajr al-Jadid reflected the government's unease about terrorism outside Israel and the Arab states.
tripoli_details: The Tripoli daily al-Fajr al-Jadid on November 14, 1972 ran a report on 'Secret Decisions of the American Government against Arabs Residing in the United States,' which the embassy called an authoritative mouthpiece for the regime.
Qadhafi gave an October 7 speech in Tripoli praising the Japanese perpetrators of the Lod Airport massacre.
Libya granted asylum to commandos freed by the Lufthansa hijackers.

frus-1981-88v24-d252.summary: In this January 9, 1986 cable the U.S. Ambassador in Rabat reported an audience with Morocco's King Hassan on dealing with Libya after President Reagan's January 7 announcement on terrorism. Hassan said Qadhafi was deeply frightened and had phoned him, and said he was sending Royal Counselor Guedira to Tripoli.
tripoli_details: Hassan said he was sending Royal Counselor Reda Guedira to Tripoli on January 9 to see what Qadhafi would do.
The ambassador told Hassan the U.S. wanted a halt to Libyan behavior, including expulsion of Abu Nidal.
He noted that Qadhafi first praised the December 27 terrorist attacks in Rome and Vienna and only later condemned them.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d53.summary: This February 13, 1970 CIA intelligence memorandum is an assessment of Libya's new military regime. It says the junta was still insecure, noted that the ministers of defense and interior were arrested in December 1969, and reported that 1,500 to 2,000 Egyptian soldiers were stationed in Benghazi and Tripoli.
tripoli_details: Some 1,500 to 2,000 Egyptian soldiers were stationed in Benghazi and Tripoli, beginning in December 1969, with about 500 more in military, security and communications posts.
In December 1969 the ministers of defense and interior were arrested before they could make a planned move against their colleagues.
The memo said the Egyptian units could keep control of an air- or beach-head if foreign moves were made to topple the regime.
It noted the quick U.S. decision to meet Libyan demands to evacuate Wheelus Air Base.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d43.summary: In Telegram 711 of June 18, 1975, the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli sent its annual policy assessment for Libya. It judged that the main danger of a Soviet military presence in Libya was that it strengthened Qadhafi's hand against a peaceful Arab-Israeli settlement, and that the regime's basic anti-communist orientation had not changed.
tripoli_details: The embassy believed the regime's basic anti-communist orientation would not change as long as Qadhafi was in power.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d124.summary: In this January 19, 1980 cable the U.S. chargé, Eagleton, reported that he called on Ahmad Shahati, head of Libya's Foreign Liaison Office, asking to be received by Qadhafi to deliver a message from President Carter. Shahati was noncommittal, though he asked whether this was the time to get 'the aircraft' passed through Congress.
tripoli_details: Eagleton said he could go to Benghazi to see Qadhafi at any time, and that Ali al Houdairi was due in Tripoli January 26.
Shahati joked or half-joked that Qadhafi would receive the American representative if the Americans in Tripoli set up a 'People's Bureau.'
Eagleton read the Afghanistan portion of Carter's message to Shahati, and said Qadhafi was to be interviewed by Harry Reasoner of CBS in Benghazi a week later.
Eagleton said he was reachable for a few days through the U.S. Embassy in Tunis.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d203.summary: This June 19, 1979 cable from the U.S. Embassy in Rome reports Under Secretary Newsom's June 18 meeting in Tunis with Tunisian Prime Minister Nouira after Newsom's visit to Tripoli. Nouira described cool Tunisian-Libyan relations, supported the U.S. ban on aircraft exports to Libya, and doubted Qadhafi would moderate.
tripoli_details: Newsom had been asked to visit Tripoli to discuss relations following Libyan messages, most recently conveyed through Marshal Tito.
Nouira supported the U.S. export ban on aircraft for Libya.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d96.summary: This October 21, 1978 State Department cable reports Acting Secretary Newsom's meeting with Libyan Foreign Secretary Turayki. They discussed Chad, southern Africa and Libya's image in Congress as a supporter of terrorism, and the meeting ended cordially with Turayki suggesting a visit to Tripoli.
tripoli_details: Newsom said a recent Arab-American Dialogue held in Tripoli had served a useful function.
Turayki suggested that Newsom or the Secretary visit Tripoli.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d143.summary: In this December 9, 1980 cable the State Department told posts about its reply to a Libyan protest over U.S. military maneuvers in Egypt. Washington said the exercises were not hostile to Libya and urged both Egypt and Libya to show restraint along their border, while noting the note's tone did not match earlier hints of improved relations.
tripoli_details: The Department said that when the U.S. representative returned from Tripoli he had indicated the Jamahiriya wanted improved relations, which the tone of the protest note did not bear out.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d93.summary: This October 17, 1972 cable reports Secretary Rogers' meeting with Libyan Foreign Minister Kikhia. Kikhia said the main problem was the U.S. failure to deliver contracted F-5 aircraft, while Rogers said the U.S. was concerned about apparent Libyan interference in other states and about terrorism.
tripoli_details: Kikhia said Libya's Mirage inventory was supposed to reach 100 but then stood at about 30.

Kikhia said that after the Wheelus agreement Libya concluded there should be no remaining complications with the U.S., and that more than 80 percent of petroleum activity in Libya was by U.S. companies.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d29.summary: On November 23, 1973 Assistant Secretary Newsom sent Kissinger a briefing memo on possible pressure points against Libya. He concluded the U.S. had little leverage, listing options from breaking relations to freezing assets, denying export licenses and banning oil-industry equipment, and warning most could provoke nationalization of remaining U.S. oil holdings.
tripoli_details: The memo said about 2,000 Americans lived in Libya, mostly oil company employees and dependents.
It said Libya had been without a Foreign Minister for nearly a year and its Embassy in Washington had been headed by a junior first secretary for more than six months.
It reported about seven hundred Libyan students in the United States.
It judged there was no identifiable focus of dissidence in Libya around which a political action program could be built.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d3.summary: In this February 18, 1977 cable the U.S. Embassy in Tunis reported a Tunisian-Libyan dispute over an Italian drilling ship working off the coast on the continental shelf. Libya's Prime Minister Jallud reportedly warned that Libyan forces would 'open fire' if Tunisia did not stop 'occupying' the rig.
tripoli_details: On Jan 18 the Libyan Foreign Ministry sent a circular note to all diplomatic missions in Tripoli except Tunisia's about the drilling operation, and a second note on Feb 1 with corrected coordinates.
On February 17 Jallud called in the Tunisian High Representative in Tripoli and threatened that Libyan forces would 'open fire.'
The drilling ship was the Scarabeo Four, owned by an AGIP/SAIPEM subsidiary of Italy's ENI.
